title: Minimum wage 18 year old NSW: How to convert hourly to annual pay
description: Learn about the minimum wage for an 18-year-old in NSW, how to convert hourly rates to annual salary, and understand tax, super, and casual loading.
salarySummary: For a full-time adult on the National Minimum Wage of $26.44/hour working 38 hours per week, the annual gross pay is about $52,269.

faqs.q: What is the minimum wage for an 18-year-old in NSW?
faqs.a: There is no single minimum wage for 18-year-olds in NSW. The National Minimum Wage ($26.44/hour from 1 July 2026) applies to adults not covered by an award. For juniors, each award sets a percentage of the adult rate based on age. For example, under the General Retail Industry Award an 18-year-old may receive 70% of the adult rate. Check the Fair Work Ombudsman pay guides for your specific award.

faqs.q: How do I convert my hourly rate to an annual salary?
faqs.a: Multiply your hourly rate by your weekly hours (typically 38 for full-time) and then by 52 weeks. For example, $30/hour × 38 × 52 = $59,280 gross per year. This assumes no unpaid leave, overtime, or allowances. Use our timesheet tool for a quick calculation.

faqs.q: Is superannuation included in my hourly rate?
faqs.a: No, super is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% (from 1 July 2026) of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830. Your employer adds this to your super fund, not to your take-home pay.

bodyMarkdown:
## Converting your hourly rate to annual pay

If you're an employee in Australia, understanding how your hourly wage translates to an annual salary is essential for budgeting and comparing job offers. The standard formula is straightforward: multiply your hourly rate by the number of hours you work each week, then multiply by 52 weeks per year. For full-time employees, the typical week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. However, part-time or casual workers may have different weekly hours.

For example, if you earn the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour (from 1 July 2026) and work 38 hours a week, your annual gross pay is approximately:

$26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,269.44

This is before tax, Medicare levy, and any other deductions. Your fortnightly gross pay would be $26.44 × 38 × 2 = $2,009.84.

### The National Minimum Wage versus award rates

The National Minimum Wage is the base minimum for employees not covered by an award or registered agreement. However, most employees in Australia are covered by an industry or occupation award, which often sets higher minimum rates. Awards also include junior rates for employees under 21, which are a percentage of the adult rate. This is particularly relevant when searching for the **minimum wage 18 year old nsw** – there is no single figure because it depends on the specific award that applies to your job.

For instance, an 18-year-old working in retail under the General Retail Industry Award may receive a certain percentage of the adult rate, while someone in hospitality under the Hospitality Industry Award will have a different percentage. The Fair Work Ombudsman provides pay guides for each award, which you can access via our [pay guides](/blog) page. Always check the correct award for your role.

### Casual loading and superannuation

If you are a casual employee, you are entitled to a casual loading of 25% on top of your base hourly rate. This loading compensates for the lack of paid leave entitlements. For example, the casual National Minimum Wage is $33.05 per hour ($26.44 + 25%). When converting to annual pay, you would use the casual rate if you work casual hours.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings. The super guarantee rate is 12% (from 1 July 2026) of your ordinary time earnings, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. Super is not deducted from your hourly rate; it is an additional cost for your employer. So if your hourly rate is $30, your employer pays an extra $3.60 per hour into your super fund.

### Tax and take-home pay

Your annual gross pay is subject to income tax and the Medicare levy. For the 2026–27 financial year, the tax-free threshold is $18,200. The tax rates are:

- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on excess over $18,200
- $45,001 – $135,000: 30% on excess over $45,000
- $135,001 – $190,000: 37% on excess over $135,000
- $190,001+: 45% on excess over $190,000

Medicare levy is generally 2% of taxable income. For a single person earning $52,269, the tax would be approximately $6,697 (using the 2026–27 rates) plus Medicare of $1,045, leaving a take-home pay of about $44,527 per year. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimator for a more precise calculation.

### Comparing with average earnings

The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) publishes Average Weekly Earnings. For May 2026, full-time adult ordinary time earnings in New South Wales were $2,108.80 per week. This is an average across all industries and occupations, not a median for any specific job. Your pay may be higher or lower depending on your role, experience, and award.

### Using the timesheet calculator

Our [the timesheet](/) tool lets you enter your base hourly rate and optionally add 25% casual loading. It then calculates your annual, fortnightly, and weekly gross pay, along with estimated tax and super. Remember to enter your base rate without casual loading – the checkbox adds it for you.

### Understanding the formula in detail

The conversion formula `hourly rate × hours per week × 52` is the standard method used by employers and the Fair Work Ombudsman. It assumes you work the same number of hours every week for 52 weeks. If you take unpaid leave, your actual annual pay will be lower. For part-time workers, use your agreed weekly hours. For casuals, hours can vary, so the annual figure is an estimate based on your typical weekly hours.

### Fortnightly pay

Many Australian employers pay fortnightly. To find your gross fortnightly pay, multiply your weekly pay by 2. Using the National Minimum Wage example: $1,004.90 per week × 2 = $2,009.80 per fortnight. This is useful for budgeting if you are paid on a fortnightly cycle.

### Junior rates and the minimum wage for 18-year-olds in NSW

The phrase **minimum wage 18 year old nsw** often leads to confusion because there is no single state minimum wage. Instead, the Fair Work system uses national awards. The National Minimum Wage applies to adult employees (21 and over) not covered by an award. For juniors, each award specifies a percentage of the adult rate based on age. For example, under the General Retail Industry Award, an 18-year-old receives 70% of the adult rate (as of current rates, but check the latest pay guide). Therefore, the minimum wage for an 18-year-old in NSW depends entirely on the award that covers their job.

To find the correct rate, visit the Fair Work Ombudsman website and use the Pay Check tool, or refer to our [pay guides](/blog) for links to award summaries. Always verify with the official source.

### Casual loading example

If you are a casual employee on the National Minimum Wage, your hourly rate including casual loading is $33.05. Using the formula: $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,318.80 annual gross. Your employer also pays super on top of this amount (12% of $65,318.80 = $7,838.26, but only up to the maximum contribution base). Note that super is not deducted from your pay; it is an additional contribution.

### Tax calculation example

For a single resident earning $65,318.80 (casual National Minimum Wage), the tax would be:
- $0 – $18,200: nil
- $18,201 – $45,000: 15% on $26,800 = $4,020
- $45,001 – $65,318.80: 30% on $20,318.80 = $6,095.64
Total tax = $10,115.64
Medicare (2%) = $1,306.38
Take-home = $65,318.80 - $10,115.64 - $1,306.38 = $53,896.78

This is an estimate. Use our [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) calculator for your specific situation.

### Super guarantee and maximum contribution base

The super guarantee rate is 12% of ordinary time earnings. However, super is only required on earnings up to the maximum contribution base, which for 2026–27 is $270,830. If your annual earnings exceed this, your employer does not have to pay super on the excess. For most workers, this cap is not reached, but it's important for high earners.

### Important disclaimer

Annual pay here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.
